Property size classifications

For a given day, a Property is deemed

(i) "Normal" if such Property has collected and processed fewer than 25 billion Events,
(ii) "Large" if such Property has collected and processed 25 billion or more Events, and
(iii) "XL" if such Property has collected and processed 250 billion or more Events, in each case, in the prior 31 day period (excluding the applicable given day (in the Property's timezone)).

Notwithstanding the foregoing, a Property may be deemed "XL" for a given day if such Property has collected and processed an average of 15 billion or more Events per day over the prior 7 day period (excluding the applicable given day (in the Property's timezone)). For purposes of the Reporting SLA and Data Processing SLA under the GA 360 SLAs, the largest size classification given to GA4 Property under this paragraph in a calendar month period will determine the corresponding GA 360 SLA tier and/or availability for such Property over the same applicable calendar month.

# Understand import sources

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/14243300?hl=en

---

Understand import sources

A import source is a container that holds the data you upload to Analytics, and comprises the database, service, or CSV file you upload and a mapping of Analytics fields to the fields in your external database, service, or CSV. Import sources control how uploaded data gets joined with existing data. You configure import sources at the property level.

To manage the import sources for a property, click Admin, then under Data collection and modification, click Data import.

On this page

Data-source types
Data-source schema
Data-source types

A data-source type corresponds to the specific type of data you want to import. For example, there are data-source types for:

campaign data
item data
user data
event data

For each one, you have different options for the dimensions and metrics (the schema) you can upload data for. Depending on the import source, you can choose to:

Upload a CSV
Use SFTP
Connect to Salesforce (Learn more).
Import offline Salesforce data
Data-source schema

When you create a source, you define a schema, the structure that joins the data you upload with the existing Analytics event data. A simple schema consists of a join-key dimension (the "key") and the import dimension(s) or metric(s). To import data, Analytics looks for key values in event data that match key values in the uploaded data. When Analytics finds a match, it adds (or replaces if data was already collected) the additional dimension and metric values associated with that key to the existing event data. Some data-source types let you use multiple dimensions to define the key, and most can use multiple dimensions/metrics for the import fields.

The join key is composed of at least one Analytics dimension, and can be composed of up to three.

The key dimensions vary based on the type of data set you choose.

A list of available key dimensions is provided in the drop-down menu in the data-source schema builder.

You can upload data via the same import source multiple times as long as you are adding values to existing fields. Once you save a import source, you can't change the mapping of Analytics fields to the fields in your import. If you want to add fields to an existing import source, you need to delete the existing import source and then create a new one. Otherwise, you can import an additional import source with the new fields you would like to include. Learn more about limits per data import type.

When you re-import data into an existing import source, previously imported data will persist while appending new imported data. If the imported data has the same set of keys as previously imported data, the data will be overwritten.

# [GA4] Verify and update consent settings in Google Analytics

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/14275483?hl=en

---

[GA4] Verify and update consent settings in Google Analytics
This article is for customers who use Google's online and offline solutions and receive data from end users in the European Economic Area (EEA).

As a part of Google's ongoing commitment to a privacy-centric digital advertising ecosystem, we are strengthening the enforcement of our EU user consent policy (EU UCP).

Advertisers must adhere to the EU UCP to use ad personalization and for measurement when using:

Tags that send data to Google (websites)
SDKs that send data to Google (apps)

To keep using applicable tags/SDKs for measurement, and for ad personalization, and remarketing features, you must collect consent for use of personal data from end users based in the EEA and share consent signals with Google for these use cases.

The requirements also apply if you are using Google Analytics data in Google Ads, Search Ads 360, or Display & Video 360. When using tools to upload data from non-Google sources, such as enhanced conversions for leads or store sales, advertisers should review our customer data policies.

Affected Analytics features

If you are using Analytics data with a Google service, such as Google Ads, Play, Display & Video 360 or others, and you take no action, only end users outside the EEA will be included in audiences used by your linked advertising products starting early March, 2024.

Review your Analytics properties to learn if you are sending the necessary consent signals to Google. Notifications in your Analytics property will guide you to your next steps. Go to the next section on this page to check if an Analytics property is receiving consent signals.

Check if Analytics is receiving consent signals

Overview

Creating and managing conversions
Create conversions based on key events so you can view the same conversion data across Google Ads and Analytics

A conversion is created from a Google Analytics event and provides a consistent way of measuring important actions in both Google Analytics and Google Ads. A conversion helps you improve your marketing strategy by providing consistent conversion counts across platforms so you can understand and optimize your ad campaigns. Conversions based on Google Analytics events allow you to measure important actions that originate from organic channels like search, email, and social for cross-channel campaign measurement use cases.

The following flow shows how to create a conversion from a Google Analytics key event: Event -> Key Event -> Conversion.

Conversion management is streamlined across Google Ads and Google Analytics for a unified cross-channel experience. This enables you to create conversions directly from your Google Analytics events and seamlessly share them with Google Ads (some settings like conversion window and counting method might not be editable in Google Ads), manage conversion settings for both products from a centralized interface, use categorized lists and detailed settings review, and track all conversion changes within Google Analytics change history.

# Tagging best practices to avoid unassigned, (not set), and direct traffic issues

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/14847402?hl=en

---

Tagging best practices to avoid unassigned, (not set), and direct traffic issues

Google Analytics tags have several configuration options that can affect session and user identity. If they are not correctly configured, it can lead to traffic sources not being able to be identified or categorized, and other issues in reports. Correct configuration successfully supports accurate reports and prevents unassigned rows in channel groups, (not set) values, and an unexpectedly large portion of traffic categorized as direct.

The unassigned row appears when Analytics cannot categorize the source of traffic (no predefined rule matches, or missing session/user identity information).

Best practices for tag code ordering: initialize the Google tag before calling an event method (including audience-triggered events); for Google Tag Manager follow the 4 setup steps; for server-side tagging don't maintain both server-side and standalone client-side implementations for the same property. Provide all relevant configuration for the page as part of the config command as early as possible, before any events. Avoid firing custom events before the config command, or they'll be batched with session_start and the page view/events won't be associated correctly.

What happens if events aren't ordered correctly: can affect user ID/session ID, causing data to appear as (not set), incorrect user/session counts, and improper measurement.

Common causes of unexpected timing: server-side tagging with Server Managed Setting substituting a different client ID (ensure all measurements flow through the server tag); cookie name customization (cookie_prefix) — use one consistent prefix across your site; automatic cross-domain linker adopting session data late (don't customize client/session ID); manual cross-domain linker APIs (client_id, session_id) being inadvertently modified — use user_id for custom user identity instead, and never manually set client/session IDs except in rare cross-domain cases.

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/14896117?hl=en

---

Advertising and attribution
About cross-channel budgeting
This feature may not be available to your Google Analytics property.

Google Analytics cross-channel budgeting helps you optimize your paid channel investments and track performance across channels.

Projections: help identify areas for improvement and make in-flight optimization decisions, monitoring how advertising channels are projected to perform against KPIs like budget, conversions, and revenue.
Scenarios: help analyze predicted ROI at different budget levels and create optimized media plans for future initiatives based on your defined budget.

Benefits: evaluate cross-channel budgets with data-driven insights; monitor in-flight pacing weekly; plan comprehensive annual/quarterly media plans. These tools are for planning purposes only and won't affect budgets or spend in connected accounts.

To view budgeting, set up the Advertising section (link to Google Ads, set up conversions) — desktop version only. Sign in > Advertising > Budgeting dropdown.

Budgeting overview page: shows recently created/modified plans, linked product links (Google Ads, DV360, etc.), cost import usage/status, and manual (third-party) integrations info.

Projection plan: helps understand how campaigns are expected to perform against a target KPI (budget, conversions, or revenue), monitor in-flight performance, and optimize budgets. Requires property eligibility and sufficient historical data. Create via Advertising > Budgeting > Projection > Create plan, name it, set planning period, choose target KPI and target value. Review shows actual performance (solid line) vs projected (dotted line) with confidence bounds; recommendations highlight most/least efficient channels.

Scenario plans: help create comprehensive quarterly/annual media plans, understand ROI at different budget levels. Requires data-driven attribution plus campaign data from linked integrations/imports. Create via Advertising > Budgeting > Scenarios > Create plan, choose target KPI (conversions or revenue), select budget estimate and conversion. Review shows a response curve for optimal budget allocation; can only start on future dates and doesn't auto-update.

Model methodologies: budgeting plans are powered by a DDA-based model (beta, GA and GA360) or Google's open-source Meridian model (alpha, select GA360 customers only).

View the data API quota history for a Google Analytics account or property

The Account data API quota history and Property data API quota history pages in the Admin section allow you to audit when users or apps access your property data through a Google Analytics API.

You can use the date picker to select a predefined or custom date range within the last 2 years. The date range is set based on your operating system's time zone.

By default, the report displays data for all users. You can apply filters to narrow your search.

Prerequisites

Viewing the data API quota history for an Analytics account or property requires the Administrator role.

This feature is to both standard and 360 properties.

View data API quota history
In Admin, under Account or Property, click Account data API quota history or Property data API quota history.
Here's a breakdown of the information listed:
Access date hour: The date hour of the Google Analytics user who accessed Google Analytics reporting data.
Accessed property name: The property display name where Google Analytics reporting data was accessed. Most Data Access Reports contain only one property, but if the requested property has a sub-property, Data Access Reports contain accesses to both the source property & sub-property. To learn more, see about sub-properties.
Accessor app name: The name of the application that accessed Google Analytics reporting data. You grant third-party apps and services access to see your Google Analytics reporting data. To learn more, see manage connections between your Google Account and third-parties.
User email: The email of the Google Analytics user that accessed Google Analytics reporting data. Some integrations allow users to access Google Analytics reporting data through the integration without the user having direct access to the property; in that case, 'userEmail' will return for example 'Google Ads Linked User' depending upon the integration.
Data API quota category: The quota category for the Data API request. Possible values include: 'Core', 'Realtime', and 'Funnel'.
Data API quota property tokens consumed: The total property quota tokens consumed for Data API requests. Learn more about quota tokens

# View the data access history for a Google Analytics account or property

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/15561150?hl=en

---

View the data access history for a Google Analytics account or property

You can use the Account data access history and Property data access history pages in the Admin section to audit when users query data in your Google Analytics properties. This includes properties within your Google Analytics account and data in your Google Ads account accessed from Google Analytics.

These pages contain the following tabs:

Data access history: Shows each instance of data access in your property or properties. It includes the access time, access mechanism, user's country location, and user's email address.
Last access time: Shows the last time each user with access to your property or properties accessed them, including API usage.

You can use the date picker to select a predefined or custom date range within the last 2 years. The date range is set based on your operating system's time zone.

By default, the report displays data for all users. You can apply filters to narrow your search.

Prerequisites

Viewing the data access history for an Analytics account or property requires the Administrator role.

This feature is available only for Google Analytics 360 properties and for accounts with at least one 360 property.

View data access history
In Admin, under Account or Property, click Account data access history or Property data access history.
The Data access history tab provides detailed information about each instance of data access. Here's a breakdown of the information listed:
Access time: The timestamp that the GA user accessed GA reporting data.
Accessed property name: The property display name where Google Analytics reporting data was accessed. Most Data Access Reports contain only one property, but if the requested property has a sub-property, Data Access Reports contain accesses to both the source property & sub-property. To learn more, see about sub-properties.
Accessor app name: The name of the application that accessed Google Analytics reporting data. You grant third-party apps and services access to see your Google Analytics reporting data. To learn more, see manage connections between your Google Account and third-parties.
Access mechanism: The mechanism through which a Google Analytics user accessed Google Analytics reporting data. Possible values include 'Google Analytics User Interface', 'Google Analytics API', 'Firebase', 'Google Ads', and others.
User country: The country of the Google Analytics user that accessed Google Analytics reporting data.

# BigQuery Fresh Daily export (GA360) - Analytics Help

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/15604391

---

# BigQuery Fresh Daily export (GA360)
 
Fresh Daily is a BigQuery export option available for 360 customers that provides faster, more complete data throughout the day than Daily or Streaming exports. Fresh Daily export data starts to arrive shortly after midnight, and typically completes by 5 AM the next day. Fresh Daily data continuously updates in batches every 60 minutes, so you can view your data faster and more reliably.

Here are some benefits of using BigQuery Fresh Daily exports:

 - Data typically arrives by 5 AM.

 - Updates are batched throughout the day, typically within 60 minutes.

 - Much faster than Daily exports.

 - More complete data than Streaming exports.

 - Same [schema](/analytics/answer/7029846#tables) as Daily exports.

 - Exports begin based on your property's timezone.

 - Uses last click observed, no modeling.

To turn on Fresh Daily exports, select **Fresh Daily **as the export type for one of your [BigQuery Links](https://analytics.google.com/analytics/web/#/?pagename=admin-integrations-big-query&utm_source=gahc&utm_medium=dlinks).

For more information on BigQuery export and to compare the Fresh Daily Export to other export types, read about [[GA4] BigQuery Export](/analytics/answer/9358801).

## Confidence and testing

For increased data confidence, you can use Fresh Daily exports alongside your existing Daily exports. For example, you can compare row counts between the two tables, which should align within 2%. Learn more about [Processing differences between Fresh Daily and Daily exports](/analytics/answer/15502882).

Fresh Daily exports contain all data fields and columns in Daily exports, including observed user attribution and Ad Impression data. Opting in to Fresh Daily exports doesn’t impact other export types. You’re billed for the additional storage cost of using additional exports. Learn more about [BigQuery pricing](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing?utm_source=support.google.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=ga4_bq_xsell_campaign&utm_content=from_page_GA4_BigQuery_Export#data_ingestion_pricing).

## Limitations

Fresh Daily is available only for [Analytics 360](/analytics/answer/14985986) "Normal" and "Large" properties. This export option is not available for "XL" premium properties. To configure Fresh Daily export, you must have billing set up on Google Cloud Platform.

 
 
**While the Fresh Daily export is stable and generally available, the Service Level Agreement on the BigQuery Fresh Daily export is not currently available.**

 

For more information on the guaranteed timing for Analytics 360 BigQuery exports, read about [[GA4] BigQuery Export

# Use audiences for advanced reporting

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/16103422?hl=en

---

Use audiences for advanced reporting

In Google Analytics, when you need to report on segments of users defined by more advanced conditions than the ones supported in the comparison feature, you can leverage audiences. Once created, these audiences can be used to define comparisons in your reports, enabling you to analyze the performance of your website or app, for different groups of users.

Create an audience

An audience can be created with a set of advanced conditions including event based, sequencing and exclusions. After you create an audience, it accumulates users who meet the conditions from that point onward.

To create an audience:
In Admin, under Data display, click Audiences.
Click New audience.
You have three options for creating an audience:
Create a new audience by defining all the parameters yourself.
Use a template and modify the existing parameters.
Select a suggested audience. You can use it as is, or modify it to suit your needs.
Use an audience to create a comparison
In Admin, under Data display, click Comparisons.
Click New comparison.
Set the comparison condition as dimension = “Audience name”, match type = “exactly matches” and value = the name of the audience you created.
Click Save and give the comparison a recognizable name.

Now, across all reports, you can apply the comparison you just created to analyze how this group of users behaves compared with other users.

Note:
Comparisons with an audience condition only include data from the moment the audience was created. This is different from regular comparisons, which can be applied retroactively to all your GA4 data.
For example, if you create an audience named “foo” on February 1st and create a comparison with the condition "audience name = foo" on February 5th, the comparison will only show data from February 1st onward.

[GA4] Business objectives

Business objectives are common business goals, such as to generate leads, drive sales, increase consideration, and understand user engagement. In Google Analytics, when you choose a business objective, you’ll be able to get personalized content to support the outcomes you want.

On this page
Activate business objectives
Configure business objectives
Edit business objectives
Activate business objectives

You can activate business objectives by selecting them during the property creation process. Each business objective is associated with a collection of reports designed to help you manage related data in order to achieve your goals. There are suggested audiences for each objective designed to help you meet that goal. Your business specific needs can be customized with the help of a template, provided by suggested audiences. Additional personalized configurations and recommendations such as recommended and key events, can be activated for each business objective.

Note: Some personalized configurations can be activated for you automatically for each business objective.
Configure business objectives

You can configure business objectives after you’ve created your property:

In Admin, under Property, select Property details.
Note: The previous link opens to the last Google Analytics property you accessed. You must be signed in to a Google Account to open the property. You can change the property using the property selector. You must be an Editor or above on the Google Analytics accountto configure your business objectives.
Select the applicable business goals in the “Business objectives (required)” field:
Generate leads
Drive sales
Understand web and/or app traffic
View user engagement & retention
Other business objectives
Click Save.
Edit business objectives

You can make the following changes to your business objectives at any time without impacting your existing enablements and data:

Deactivate or reactivate automatically enabled features
Change from one business objective to another

If you don’t have any specific business objectives, you can set them to Other business objectives.

# Syncing subproperties

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/16176212?hl=en

---

Syncing subproperties

Subproperties are available only to Google Analytics 360 accounts that are linked to a Google Marketing Platform organization with an active 360 order. Only a Google Analytics 360 property can be the source property for a subproperty.

Sync a subproperty to its source property so that it can use custom dimensions and custom metrics configured in the source property.

How it works

After syncing, the subproperty can only use the dimensions and metrics already defined in the source, and can’t edit, remove, or create new ones. Updates from the source are automatically reflected in the subproperty. When unsynced, the subproperty retains a copy and can edit these custom dimensions and custom metrics.

Note: Syncing isn’t available for roll-up properties. Learn more about roll-up properties.

Initial syncing can take up to 48 hours. Once they are ready to be used, the status will update to “Synced” in the source property’s Admin > Subproperty management.

Note: You can opt-in to sync a subproperty during the subproperty creation stage, or sync an existing subproperty that has no custom dimensions or custom metrics. To create a subproperty, you must be an Editor or above on the Analytics account, and the source property must be an ordinary property. You can’t create a subproperty from another subproperty or a roll-up property. Learn more about how to Create and edit subproperties.
Create and sync a subproperty
In Admin, under Property, click Subproperty management > Create a subproperty.
Note: The previous link opens to the last Google Analytics property you accessed. You must be signed in to a Google Account to open the property. You can change the property using the property selector. You must be an Editor or above on the Google Analytics account to create a subproperty.
Select a 360 source property under the Source property name menu.
Enter a name for the subproperty and select the timezone and currency.
Select “I'm aware of the additional cost in creating this property”, then click Next.
Click Edit filter to configure the include and/or exclude conditions that define which event data from the source property appears in the subproperty.
When you've finished configuring the conditions for the filter, click Confirm, then click Next.
Under Choose what to sync to the subproperty, click the toggle next to Sync all custom dimensions and custom metrics to the subproperty.
Click Next.
Select an industry category for the subproperty, the size of the business you measure with the subproperty, and the reasons you use Analytics.
Click Create.
Check subproperty sync status
In Admin, under Property, click Subproperty management.
Check the Sync

# Prepare your data for import

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/16308305?hl=en

---

Prepare your data for import
Learn how to prepare your data for successful import.

This article applies to supported import sources that are part of an open beta and are subject to change.

Keep your data fresh

You must ensure your data is refreshed in the import source before a manual or scheduled import source connection runs in order for that data to be imported for use in the intended destination or use case. For example, if you choose a daily schedule, you need to refresh your data on a daily basis, before the scheduled start time.

Make your data available

When connecting to an import source, each use case you want to implement should have its own dedicated table or a filtered subset of table data within that source. You can reuse the same table from a connected import source for multiple use cases by using different filtered subsets of that table.

Some import sources require you to have proper credentials in order to make the import source connection. See the specific guide for the import source you're using for specific guidance.

Format your data

The following sections show you how to properly format your data, to ensure it can be imported without error.

About file formats

If you are uploading a file, such as a CSV file, the first line of the file must contain the headers.

Ensure that the file has an extension, as files without extensions are rejected.

About date and time formats

Converting dates and times of various formats into a logical timestamp is supported and should be based on six templates using three format sets: DATE, TIME, and TIMEZONE. The DATETIME type is not supported. DATETIME fields need to be converted to the STRING type in the import source, using the supported formats described in this article.

The following are examples of timestamps in supported formats:

2012-08-15T00:01:54Z (UTC ISO 8601 Standard)
2012-08-14T17:01:54-07:00 (ISO 8601 Standard with Offset)
Aug 14, 2012 17:01:54
08/14/2012T5:01:54 PM
2012-08-14 5:01:54 PM
08/14/2012 17:01:54
2012-08-14 17:01:54
08/14/2012 17:01:54*123
2012-08-14T17:01:54-07
08/14/2012T17:01:54-0700
2012-08-14T17:01:54-070000
2012-08-14T17:01:54-07:00:00
2012-08-14T17:01:54 America/Los_Angeles
Aug 14, 2012 17:01:54PST
2012-08-14 17:01:54 PST
2012-08-14 17:01:54 Pacific Standard Time
2012-08-14 17:01:54 GMT-07:00
08/14/2012 17:01:54 GMT-07:00:00
July 17, 2025 17:01:54 PST
17 July 2025 17:01:54 GMT-07:00
17-Jul-2025T17:01:54-07:00

When you import data, Analytics automatically converts various common date formats into the ISO 8601 standard, YYYY-MM-DD.

The following formats are supported for date fields:

Format	Description	Example
YYYY-MM-DD	ISO 8601	2025-07-17
MM/DD/Y

# Troubleshoot diagnostics for web purchase events

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/16729583?hl=en

---

Troubleshoot diagnostics for web purchase events

Issues with data collected via Google tag, Measurement Protocol, or data import sources trigger diagnostic alerts on the Data streams and Data import pages.

Diagnostics in Data streams: Admin > Data collection and modification > Data streams; a badge reflects diagnostic status; select the stream, go to Diagnostics tab, click the alert's CTA link (Editor+ required to resolve).

Diagnostics in Data import: Admin > Data import; badge on the data source; click the arrow icon, view alerts under "Connection quality", click the CTA link.

Diagnostic statuses: No issues detected / Excellent (no issues found); Needs attention (an issue affecting measurement, not critical); Urgent (critical issue needing immediate fix).

# Troubleshoot diagnostics for problematic User-ID implementations

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/16757557?hl=en

---

Troubleshoot diagnostics for problematic User-ID implementations

Setting user IDs accurately matters for GA data/reporting accuracy. User-ID lets you associate your own identifiers with individual users to connect behavior across sessions/devices/platforms; Analytics treats each user ID as a separate user for more accurate counts.

To send user IDs: create a unique ID per user yourself (typically at login, e.g. derived from email), consistently reassign it, and keep each ID at 256 characters or fewer.

When User-ID is set incorrectly, impact can include misattribution across reports and a permanent effect on historical data.

Note: you're responsible for complying with the GA Terms of Service — avoid impermissible PII in the user ID, disclose identifier use in your Privacy Policy, and ensure the ID can't be used by a third party to determine a user's identity.

Diagnostics: a global banner appears if the implementation is causing limits to be reached (data impacted); a Data quality indicator appears in affected reports.

# Troubleshoot diagnostics for parameter stripping

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/16973975?hl=en

---

Troubleshoot diagnostics for parameter stripping

Aggregate identifiers (GBRAID and gad_ parameters) are used by GA to attribute paid traffic to traffic source dimensions when GCLID can't be used (e.g. when users deny ad_user_data consent). The parameter stripping diagnostic flags when these appended click-URL parameters are being stripped, hurting aggregate-identifier-based attribution coverage.

All property users can view diagnostics; only Editor+ can resolve them. Fixes take up to 48 hours to reflect.

Effect on property: stripped parameters cause inaccurate attribution, showing as "(not set)" or "organic" in reports; properties lose the benefit of GBRAID/gad_-based mitigation.

Diagnostics in reports: appears in the Data quality indicator when GBRAID or gad_ are missing from URLs that do have GCLID.

Diagnostic alert: "Campaign data accuracy is affected by missing URL parameters" — some URLs are missing GBRAID and/or gad_. To resolve: fix the implementation preventing these auto-added parameters from reaching Analytics (view problematic paths via View URLs); changes take 24-48h to take effect.

Lets you create custom visualizations to pull actionable insights from GA data into a single consolidated page, directly within the GA interface.

Limitations: standard properties max 15 cards/dashboard, premium properties max 30; all published dashboards are shared with the whole property; API support, segments, and card-level comparisons aren't supported yet.

About Google Ads list size estimates in Google Analytics


# About Google Ads list size estimates in Google Analytics

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/17456279?hl=en

---

About Google Ads list size estimates in Google Analytics

When building audiences in GA for remarketing, this feature gives real-time estimates of an audience's eligibility across Google Ads networks at creation time, to avoid creating audiences too small to serve.

Measurement size (GA) vs Google Ads estimated size (Advertising): GA measurement size is the total users meeting your criteria (reporting/analytical). Google Ads estimated size is the remarketable portion of that audience — smaller, due to consent choices, cookie availability, browser limits, or lack of Google identifier matches. These two numbers are not expected to match.

How it works: ML models forecast list size 30 days ahead, shown as a range representing a 60% confidence interval (20th-80th percentile). Real-time estimates cover 4 channels: Search, YouTube, Display, Gmail.

Status indicators (probability audience is too small): Green "Likely large enough to serve" (<8% risk); Yellow "May be too small to serve" (8-20% risk, consider widening criteria/duration); Red "Likely too small to serve" (>20% risk, modify parameters). Minimum requirement today: 100 active users in the last 30 days (also 100 minimum for Display/YouTube/Gmail networks).

Eligibility requirements: property must be linked to an active Google Ads account with Ads Personalization enabled, and have sufficient traffic for the prediction models.

"No Prediction" reasons: no Google Ads link; predictions not yet ready (newly linked/calibrating); low prediction confidence (too much variance or too-unique segment criteria).

How to maximize list sizes: widen audience conditions (relax AND chains / use OR); increase membership duration (up to 540 days); implement User-Provided Data (hashed emails etc.) to improve matching, especially in privacy-restricted browsers; ensure consent mode is properly implemented (ad_personalization signal) so remarketable traffic is correctly identified.

# [GA4] Policy requirements for Google Analytics Advertising Features

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2700409?hl=en

---

[GA4] Policy requirements for Google Analytics Advertising Features
(Applies to both GA4 and Universal Analytics.)

Advertising Features let you enable capabilities not available in standard implementations: Remarketing with Google Analytics, Google Display Network Impression Reporting, Demographics and Interest Reporting, and integrated services requiring GA to collect data via advertising cookies/identifiers for ad purposes.

Enabling Advertising Features means GA collects traffic data via Google advertising cookies/identifiers in addition to standard data, regardless of how you send data to GA (tracking code, SDK, Measurement Protocol) — this policy applies whenever Advertising Features are used.

You are the sole data controller under applicable data protection law. Linking your Analytics property to Google Ads enables data flow between them: data exported to Ads is governed by Ads ToS; data imported from Ads into Analytics is governed by Analytics ToS.

You must not identify users or merge PII with data from any Google advertising product/feature unless you have robust notice and the user's prior opt-in consent, and are using a GA feature that expressly supports such identification/merger. You must never attempt to disaggregate data Google reports in aggregate, regardless of consent.

Privacy policy disclosure required if Advertising Features are enabled: which features you use; how first-party (GA cookie) and third-party (Google ad cookies) identifiers are used together; how visitors can opt out (Ads Settings, Ad Settings for mobile apps, or other means like NAI opt-out). Also point users to GA's web opt-outs.

Must also comply with the EU User Consent Policy when using Advertising Features. For Japan: non-PII user info received from Google about Japanese users can't be merged with PII without prior legally-required consent and disclosure to Google via the Troubleshooter.

Interest-based advertising (including Remarketing): must follow policies of the linked Google services (e.g. Google Ads Personalized advertising policy and sensitive-category restrictions). Can't use GA to collect sensitive-category data for interest-based advertising purposes; interest-based advertising can be disabled via the advanced ads-personalization setting.

Policy last updated May 16, 2024.

[UA] IP masking in Universal Analytics [Legacy]


# [UA] IP masking in Universal Analytics [Legacy]

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2763052?hl=en

---

[UA] IP masking in Universal Analytics [Legacy]
(Legacy article about Universal Analytics. In GA4, IP masking is unnecessary since IP addresses aren't logged or stored.)

At a glance: when a UA customer requests IP-address masking, Analytics truncates the address as soon as technically feasible — last octet of IPv4 (or last 80 bits of IPv6) is set to zero in memory shortly after receipt, before writing to disk. Geographic dimensions are derived from the truncated address. In UA, IP masking is opt-in.

In depth: the anonymize_ip feature (gtag('config', ID, {anonymize_ip: true})) lets site owners request masking of all users' IPs, to help comply with privacy policies/local DPA recommendations. Truncation happens before any storage/processing.

Pipeline: (1) Analytics JavaScript Tag — when the config/tracking function fires, it sends data as URL params to the /collect endpoint; if masking was called first, an &aip=1 parameter is added. (2) Analytics Collection Network — servers serving gtag.js and collecting /collect requests; the request (with HTTP/TCP-IP headers including requester IP) is held in memory; if &aip=1 is present, the IP's last octet (IPv4) or last 80 bits (IPv6) is zeroed in memory before the request is written to disk — e.g. 12.214.31.144 becomes 12.214.31.0. The full IP is never written to disk when this is used.

Data Processing Terms

The Google Ads Data Processing Terms are for businesses affected by GDPR or similar regulations, and supersede the previous Google Analytics Data Processing Amendment (including the German version).

GA customers with a direct customer contract can accept the Google Ads Data Processing Terms in Account Settings. Standard/360 customers established outside EEA/UK/Switzerland must proactively accept; those established in EEA/UK/Switzerland, or 360 customers who accepted the GA360 Terms of Use, already have it incorporated and don't need to act.

Exception: GA360 Sales Partners and Resale Clients (customers buying via a Sales Partner) are not eligible to accept via the UI — they need separate data processing terms with Google or their Sales Partner; UI acceptance by them is invalid.

Accept the amendment (requires Editor role at account level): Admin > correct account > Account Settings > Account details > Data Processing Amendment > Review Amendment > Done > Done again. Only applies to pre-existing accounts; new accounts auto-accept.

Required contact info after accepting: Legal Entity, Primary Contact (notification email), Data Protection Officer (if applicable), EEA Representative (if applicable).

# Demo account

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/6367342?hl=en

---

Demo account
Learn by experimenting with data from the Google Merchandise Store and Flood-It!

The GA demo account is a fully functional account any Google user can access, containing 2 (article says 2, links describe 3) properties: Google Merchandise Store (ecommerce web data) and Flood-It! (app+web game data).

Access: click a demo-account link; log in or create a Google account; this adds the demo account to your existing (or newly created) GA account. It's available from the account selector. It counts against your max-2000-accounts-per-Google-account limit. Removable at any time.

Where the data comes from: Merchandise Store data includes traffic source, content, and transaction data. Flood-It! (a puzzle game) data includes calculated metrics (ARPU, avg engagement time, Buyer conversion, Revenue heartbeat), events data (level completion/reset), and ecommerce (in-app purchase) data.

Ways to use it: view standard reporting, explore games reporting, basic analysis (channel acquisition, unique users, conversions), funnel exploration, ad-hoc drag-and-drop explorations.

BigQuery Export schema


# BigQuery Export schema

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7029846?hl=en

---

BigQuery Export schema

Explains the format/schema of GA property data and Firebase data exported to BigQuery.

Datasets: each linked GA property/Firebase project gets a single dataset named "analytics_<property_id>" in your BigQuery project (Property ID found in property settings or Firebase App Analytics Settings).

Tables: with Daily export, a table events_YYYYMMDD is created each day. With Streaming export, events_intraday_YYYYMMDD is populated continuously through the day and deleted once the corresponding events_YYYYMMDD is complete. Late-arriving events update daily tables for up to 3 days after the event date (correct timestamp preserved); events arriving after that window aren't recorded. BigQuery sandbox has no intraday import and additional limits (upgrade to get intraday imports).

Columns: each column is an event-specific parameter; some are nested in RECORDS (some, like items and event_params, are repeatable) — categories include event, user, device, geo, app_info, collected_traffic_source, session_traffic_source_last_click, traffic_source, stream/platform, ecommerce, items, publisher (early access).

Rows: one event may span multiple rows if it has repeated RECORDS — the initial row has event name/date/timestamp/non-repeated fields; the repeated event_params RECORD populates subsequent rows directly under it (e.g. a page_view event's page_location, page_title, medium, source, page_referrer each as separate event_params rows).

# BigQuery Export error messages

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7031061?hl=en

---

BigQuery Export error messages

Setup errors:
"You do not have sufficient access to the Cloud project to complete the linking process" — cause: missing permissions on the Cloud project; remedy: ask your Cloud admin for sufficient permissions (BigQuery Data Owners can create datasets/tables).
"No available dataset locations under this project" — cause: org policies block export to available regions; remedy: modify org policies to include the desired region.
"Something went wrong, please try again later" — cause unknown; remedy: retry later.

Export errors:
ACCESS_DENIED — Firebase Analytics lacks permission to the linked BigQuery Project; remedy: ensure the service account firebase-measurement@system.gserviceaccount.com has OWNER access to the BigQuery Project. Losing this access causes ongoing errors and permanent data gaps.
BILLING_ERROR — billing issue on the linked Google Cloud Account; remedy: ensure the Cloud Billing Account has a valid, up-to-date payment method. Unresolved billing issues cause ongoing errors and permanent data gaps.

For other errors, refer to Firebase support resources.

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7201382

# Monitor events in DebugView
 Monitor events from your website or mobile app as Analytics collects them 
DebugView displays the events and user properties that Analytics collects from a user in real time, allowing you to troubleshoot issues as you install your tags or step through an external user's live activity. You must enable debug mode to use DebugView.

## Enable debug mode

You can enable debug mode for the events from your personal device or for the events from all user devices. When troubleshooting your tag installation, it's best to enable debug mode for your personal device so you can easily identify your device from Debug Device in DebugView.

This section describes how to enable debug mode for a website. To enable debug mode for an Android or iOS app, see [this article](https://firebase.google.com/docs/analytics/debugview) instead.

### Enable debug mode for yourself

To enable debug mode for your personal device, use the Google Tag Assistant through [tagassistant.google.com](https://tagassistant.google.com/) or [preview mode](/tagmanager/answer/6107056). Tag Assistant adds a parameter to your website address to enable debug mode.

### Enable debug mode for everyone

To enable debug mode for all user devices, you will need to update your configuration.

 
 
## Google tag (gtag.js)

 
 
 
#### Monitor all events

 
To monitor all the events on a page, add a `'debug_mode':true` parameter to your `config` command, as follows:

 
`gtag('config', 'G-12345ABCDE', { 'debug_mode':true });`

 
#### Monitor some events

 
To monitor certain events only, add a `'debug_mode':true` parameter to just those events, for example:

 
`gtag('event', 'xyz', { 'debug_mode':true });`

 
#### Disable debug mode

 
To disable debug mode, exclude the `'debug_mode'` parameter; setting the parameter to `false` doesn't disable debug mode.

 
 
 

 
 
## Google Tag Manager

 
 
#### Monitor all events

 
To monitor activity from all website users, set `debug_mode` to `true` in your [Google tag](/tagmanager/answer/9442095#config).

 
 

 
#### Monitor some events

 
To monitor activity for certain events only, set `debug_mode` to `true` in your [Google Analytics: Google Analytics Event tag](/tagmanager/answer/9442095#event?).

 
#### Disable debug mode

 
To disable debug mode, exclude the `'debug_mode'` field. Setting the field to `false` won't disable debug mode.

 
 

## Monitor the events in DebugView

Gain deeper insights about your users and their journeys

Explorations is a collection of advanced techniques beyond standard reports for deeper insight into customer behavior: ad hoc queries, switching between techniques, sorting/drilling into data, filters/segments, creating segments/audiences, sharing, and exporting. Available on all GA properties (360 customers get a beta on Universal Analytics too).

Access: click Explore in the left navigation.

An exploration has 3 sections: Canvas (the visualization area, can have multiple tabs/techniques), Variables (left panel: dimensions/metrics/segments available, plus timeframe control), Tab Settings (configure the current tab's technique and options).

Techniques: Free-form exploration (crosstab, multiple visualization styles: bar/pie/line/scatter/geo); Cohort exploration (behavior of user groups sharing attributes); Funnel exploration (steps to complete tasks, optimize UX, find over/under-performing audiences); Segment overlap (how segments relate, find new complex-criteria segments); User exploration (examine users in a segment, drill into individual activity); Path exploration (visualize user paths); User lifetime (behavior/value over customer lifetime).

Create an exploration: blank or from a template; select a technique; add dimensions/metrics in Variables; drag them into Tab Settings; interact with the visualization; add segments/filters; export findings to Remarketing Audiences. Only the creator can delete an exploration. Can also create from a report via the comparison button > Explore.

Data retention


# Data retention

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7667196?hl=en

---

Data retention

Data Retention controls set how long user-level and event-level data (cookies, User-ID, advertising IDs like AAID/IDFA) is kept before automatic deletion.

Google-signals data is retained at most 26 months regardless of settings (defaults to 26 months, but respects a shorter Data Retention setting if configured).

Retention options: user-level data (and key events data) can be set to 2 or 14 months. Other event data can be set to 2, 14, 26 (360 only), 38 (360 only), or 50 months (360 only). Age/gender/interest data is always capped at 2 months regardless of settings. Large/XL properties are limited to 2 months. Increasing retention applies retroactively to already-collected data.

Important: the retention setting does NOT affect standard aggregated reports (even with comparisons) — it only affects Explorations and funnel reports.

Changing retention: deletion runs monthly; reducing retention deletes newly-out-of-window data on the next monthly run; increasing retention applies to existing undeleted data; a change takes effect after a 24-hour grace period during which you can revert it. Using a report date range longer than the retention period hides the extra days' data.

When a property exceeds size limits: a standard property becoming Large, or a 360 property becoming XL, automatically reduces event-level retention to 2 months (older data permanently deleted). Admins get a warning email if pacing toward the limit, and another when the limit is hit; you can reduce billable event volume to stay under the limit and keep longer retention, or upgrade to 360 for higher limits.

Reset on new activity: ON resets a user identifier's retention clock on each new event (identifier never expires while the user stays active); OFF means data is deleted strictly after the retention period regardless of activity. Applies to user-level data only.

Set options: requires Editor role. Admin > Property > Data Settings > Data Retention > choose Event data retention period and Reset user data on new activity toggle > Save.

Note on Users metric: added to many reports in Feb 2018; historical data before GA started aggregating it (360: May 1 2016; standard: Sept 1 2016) may show zeros — doesn't affect the Audience Overview report, which has long-aggregated Active user data.

Understanding PII in Google's contracts and policies


# Understanding PII in Google's contracts and policies

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7686480?hl=en

---

Understanding PII in Google's contracts and policies

Many Google advertising/measurement contracts and policies refer to "Personally Identifiable Information" (PII), which is a different categorization than the GDPR's "personal data" — data excluded from Google's PII definition may still count as personal data/information under GDPR or US state privacy laws.

This article explains how Google interprets PII when not otherwise defined in your contract, to reduce confusion versus GDPR/CPRA concepts.

What Google considers PII: information that alone could directly identify, contact, or precisely locate an individual — email addresses, mailing addresses, phone numbers, precise locations (e.g. GPS coordinates), full names or usernames. Example: a publisher barred from sending PII to Google must not include email addresses in ad-serving page URLs.

Note: certain products allow limited PII transmission under specific policies (e.g. approximate location under certain conditions) — this article doesn't override those provisions.

What Google's PII interpretation excludes: pseudonymous cookie IDs, pseudonymous advertising IDs, IP addresses, other pseudonymous end-user identifiers. E.g., an IP address sent with an ad request (inherent to internet protocols) doesn't breach a PII-sending prohibition.

Important: data excluded from Google's PII definition may still be personal data/information under GDPR and other privacy legislation — this article doesn't affect those separate legal obligations.

Privacy controls in Google Analytics


# Privacy controls in Google Analytics

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9019185?hl=en

---

Privacy controls in Google Analytics

Useful resource for site/app owners ("customers") affected by GDPR or similar regulations. See also Safeguarding your data.

Disable Analytics data collection: apps (Firebase SDK, Android SDK, iOS SDK — programmatic instructions each); web (gtag.js, programmatic) — users can also opt out via the Google Analytics opt-out browser add-on.

Disable collection of granular location/device data (per-region toggle, on by default): stops collecting City, city lat/long, browser minor version, browser User-Agent string, device brand/model/name, OS minor version, platform minor version, screen resolution. Historical data is kept; disabling significantly reduces modeled-key-events volume and impacts downstream key event modeling/reporting in linked Ads/Search Ads 360.

Redact email addresses and user-defined URL query parameters: client-side text redaction configurable on web data streams (see Data redaction).

Disable Google signals collection (per-region toggle): historical data kept, no new collection from the change forward; disabling loses remarketing lists based on third-party ad identifiers, advertising reporting, and demographics/interests, plus impacts downstream key event modeling/reporting in linked Google Ads.

Disable advertising features / advertising personalization: separate app (Firebase/Android/iOS SDK) and web (gtag.js) programmatic controls.

IP Masking: not necessary in Google Analytics (properties don't log/store IP addresses) — the setting exists historically for Universal Analytics.

Retention period: settable for GA properties and GA for Firebase (max 14 months, or default retention policy).

User-level data access/portability: via Explorations' User Explorer / User Activity report (analyze/export event-level data per user identifier, delete individual user records), or full export to BigQuery for a queryable event-data repository.

Delete end-user data on device: Firebase SDK's resetAnalyticsData (Android/iOS) deletes locally stored data and resets the app-instance ID; setAnalyticsCollectionEnabled controls per-device collection.

Delete end-user data on Analytics servers: via the Analytics User Deletion API, per-app per-device.

Allow/disable ads personalization: via the advanced "allow for ads personalization" setting, per property.

SKAdNetwork registration (iOS): unless opted out via a static config flag, the Firebase iOS SDK auto-calls Apple's SKAdNetwork registerAppForAdNetworkAttribution on first open, relevant to iOS 14+ ad-network attribution given Apple's IDFA consent requirements since WWDC 2020.

Sample queries for audiences based on BigQuery data


# Sample queries for audiences based on BigQuery data

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9037342?hl=en

---

Sample queries for audiences based on BigQuery data

After exporting Firebase/GA data to BigQuery, use these Standard SQL query templates as a basis for audience queries (modify table names/date ranges). Queries return a COUNT of users; remove the outer COUNT() to get the list of user_ids instead. Audience data from these queries is informational only, not actionable (can't be pushed back as an activation audience).

Purchasers: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM `YOUR_TABLE.events_*` WHERE event_name IN ('in_app_purchase','purchase') AND _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN 'start' AND 'end'.

N-day active users: users with an event_params.key='engagement_time_msec' > 0 within event_timestamp > NOW - INTERVAL N DAY (cross join event_params).

N-day inactive users: users active in the last M days but NOT active in the last N days (M>N) — computed via LEFT JOIN of the M-day active set against the N-day active set, keeping rows where the N-day match is NULL (BigQuery lacked EXCEPT ALL at the time).

Frequently active users: users with engagement_time_msec>0 on at least N of the last M days (GROUP BY user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT event_date) HAVING >= N).

Highly active users: users with SUM(engagement_time_msec) over the last M days exceeding N minutes (converted to microseconds: N*60*1000000).

Acquired users: filter events_* WHERE traffic_source.source/medium/name match your campaign, within a date range.

Cohorts with filters: e.g. users whose first_open event_timestamp falls 7-14 days ago AND traffic_source.source='google' — combines a cohort window with an acquisition-source filter.

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9212670?hl=en

Reports
Overview of Google Analytics reports

GA collects data from websites/apps to build reports for monitoring traffic and understanding users. Data appears first in the Realtime report, then in other reports shortly after; some data needs additional setup. All reports are under Reports in the left nav.

When you open Reports you see: Reports snapshot, Realtime report, and a number of predefined reports — everyone with GA access sees the same set on the left.

Report collections (shown below Reports snapshot/Realtime, customizable):
- App developer: key Firebase-connected app metrics — appears when you add the Firebase SDK to a connected app.
- Business objectives: tailored reports based on setup answers — appears if you picked a business objective other than "Get baseline reports".
- Data import: assess imported data — present on all properties.
- Games reporting: game-specific funnel/behavior metrics — appears if an app data stream is tied to a Play Store/App Store games app, or industry category is set to "Games".
- Life cycle: acquisition-to-retention customer journey — appears if you picked "Get baseline reports" during setup, created the property before March 27 2023, or migrated from Universal Analytics via Setup Assistant.
- User: demographics/interests/devices/app versions — present by default on all properties.

# Measure activity across platforms with User-ID

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9213390?hl=en

---

First-party data
Measure activity across platforms with User-ID

User-ID lets you associate your own identifiers with individual users to connect behavior across sessions/devices/platforms; each user ID is treated as a separate user for accurate counts. If Analytics is linked to BigQuery, user-ID data exports to BigQuery regardless of consent status.

Before you begin: generate a unique ID per user yourself (typically at login, e.g. derived from email) and reassign it consistently; max 256 characters; must comply with GA ToS (no impermissible PII, disclose use in your Privacy Policy, must not let a third party determine identity from it).

About user IDs: use a real ID (blank/dummy IDs cause inaccurate/permanently-lost data); ensure uniqueness per user — reusing an ID across users blends their data (example: John and Mary sharing "UserID123" appear as one user who viewed 2 products and purchased once, hiding that they're 2 distinct people).

Verify reporting identity: Admin > Data display > Reporting Identity (Editor+ required) — choose Blended (user ID + device ID + modeled data) or Observed (user ID + device ID).

What you can do: compare signed-in vs non-signed-in users via the "Signed in with user ID" dimension comparison; use User exploration to drill into individual users in a segment (acquisition, summary metrics, activity timeline); create remarketing audiences from User-ID data (shared to linked Google Ads — if using User-ID, only the last device's identifiers are included per logged-in user; without it, all device/user identifiers are included).

Handling incomplete User-ID collection: events before sign-in stay unassociated; once signed in, subsequent events (and the earlier unassociated ones in-session) associate with that user ID; after sign-out, subsequent events become unassociated again; signing back in with the same ID re-associates new events, but earlier post-signout events stay unassociated. JS special values: undefined = no user_id sent (same as never setting one); null = explicit logged-out state (recommended over empty string); empty string "" = also logged-out but can cause coding issues, so prefer null. Any other value (including the literal strings "undefined"/"null") is treated as a real unique user ID.

Limits: must comply with the Analytics SDK/User-ID Feature Policy; max 256 chars; historical data before implementation isn't retroactively associated; User-ID data can't be shared/mixed across properties. Ensure every user gets a unique persistent ID, never a dummy/placeholder after logout (use null), and don't accidentally start a new session per event.

Enhanced measurement lets you measure interactions with your content by enabling options (events) in the Google Analytics interface. No code changes are required. When you enable these options for a web data stream, your Google Analytics tag starts sending events right away.

Before turning on the enhanced measurement feature, be sure you understand each option and what enhanced data will be collected. You can also turn off specific measurement options in settings.

Dimensions and metrics
[GA4] Predefined user dimensions

Using the SDK or gtag.js, these user dimensions collect automatically (no extra code); all available in Audience conditions, some also as report filters. iOS apps need IDFA collected to auto-derive Age/Gender/Interests.

Dimensions: Age (bracket: 18-24...65+), App store, App version, Browser, City, Continent, Country, Device brand, Device category, Device model, Gender, Interests, Language, New/Established (app-only: New = first opened within 7 days, Established = >7 days ago), Operating system, OS version, Platform, Region, Subcontinent.

App-instance ID: auto-generated/assigned per app instance, used for user metrics; must be a 32-hex-no-dashes value or dashless RFC4122 v4 UUID or GA4 measurement protocol submissions are dropped. For unconsented data via measurement protocol, app_instance_id must be created per event. Access via getAppInstanceId; reset via resetAnalyticsData.

Data thresholds: demographic/interest data requires meeting Analytics data thresholds — Google withholds data below a minimum instance count to prevent re-identification.

Google signals: activating it gives more holistic demographic/interest data by associating event data with signed-in, ads-personalization-consented Google accounts.

Geography dimensions (City, Region, etc.) are approximated from IP address.

[GA4] Realtime report


# [GA4] Realtime report

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9271392?hl=en

---

Reports
[GA4] Realtime report
Monitor activity on your website or app as it happens

Cards: active users in last 5/30 min (per minute); active users by first source/medium/platform/campaign; active/new users by audience; views by page title/screen name; event count by event name; key events by event name; active users by user property. Realtime shows user-scoped dimensions/metrics (about how users were first acquired).

Note: cards show max 700 rows; high-cardinality dimensions may bucket into (other), causing discrepancies (see About the (other) row).

View: Reports > Realtime (Editors+ can re-add if removed from nav).

Uses: verify a promotion/campaign is driving traffic; monitor effect of a blog/social post; verify new content's traffic impact; confirm measurement code works. Best-effort service, no formal SLO, occasional delivery delays are normal.

Comparisons: create custom comparisons (e.g. age 18-24 vs overall) or click a map bubble to compare a city's users to all users.

User snapshots: View user snapshot shows a single user's device/app version/location, top events, and user properties; arrows cycle between users.

User processing: "Active in last 5/30 min" = all users in that window; "New users" = first-time users; "Active users" = returning, already-processed users (new/unprocessed users excluded from this count).

User acquisition processing: "Active users by First user source" only shows established users who've completed normal batch processing — brand-new users won't appear there yet.

App data is batched (delays on the order of minutes) to conserve battery.

Attribution: Realtime (like DebugView) does limited attribution analysis for responsiveness — use Acquisition reports for accurate attribution.

Realtime vs DebugView: Realtime covers the last 30 min only (DebugView covers longer periods in debug mode); both support web+app; Realtime comparisons show a specific stream, DebugView's DEBUG DEVICE shows a specific device; Realtime's user snapshot is random, DebugView has none; Realtime is visible to anyone with property access, DebugView is mainly for developers.

# [GA4] User explorer

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9283607?hl=en

---

[GA4] User explorer
Explore segments of users and drill into individual user activities.

Lets you select a group of users (e.g. engaged on both app and web) and drill into each individual's activity — useful for personalization or troubleshooting a specific user flow (e.g. high average-order-value users, or where a user failed to complete an order).

Create: Explore > Template Gallery > User explorer template, configure options. Or right-click a data point in an existing visualization > View users (applies current customizations as a temporary/dashed-border segment you can edit/save).

How it works: shows the users making up a segment (existing or temporary); drill into acquisition info, summary metrics, and an activity timeline per user; can create a new segment from events a user took.

Customize: only dimensions possible are Device ID and Stream Name; metrics are configurable in Tab Settings > Values. Adjust rows (Show rows / Start row, default top 10 by sessions), sort by clicking a metric column, choose Cell type (plain text, colored bars, heat maps). Apply an existing segment by dragging it into the segment target. Apply filters (multiple conditions combine with AND). Adjust time frame via the Variables calendar.

View individual activity: click a record to see acquisition detail and an event timeline. Each row = a unique "Effective user ID" (User ID if available, else Device ID — app instance ID or web client ID) per the property's reporting identity.

Customize activity list: TIMELINE section lets you show selected events, collapse/expand, and sort.

Create a segment from individual users: select one or more events in the timeline > Create Segment; editable/savable afterward.

Delete user data (irreversible): open/create a user explorer (requires Editor+), select the Effective user ID in that column, click Delete user icon, confirm in the Warning dialog. Data stops displaying within 24 hours and is permanently removed within 63 days.

Deleting by pseudonymous ID: to see all of a logged-out user's data (pseudonymous ID, distinct from their User ID when logged in — Analytics doesn't auto-associate the two, you must do so yourself), switch Reporting identity to "By device only" (Admin > Data display > Reporting identity, Editor+ required), open a new user explorer to see pseudonymous IDs, select and delete as above.

# Connect Firebase to Google Analytics

> **Fonte:** https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9289234?hl=en

---

Connect Firebase to Google Analytics

Starting from Google Analytics: create a GA4 property, then link a Firebase project to it to measure app data. One Firebase project can link to only one GA4 property (all its apps send to that single property).

Update settings after linking: Admin > Product links > Firebase links (Editor+) — adjust Firebase-user access to Analytics data, or turn off enhanced audience integration (on by default).

User access: linking auto-grants Firebase project users Analytics roles based on their highest Firebase firebaseanalytics permission, via 4 "Firebase linked user" buckets: googleAnalyticsEdit -> Firebase project Editor -> Analytics Editor (no restrictions); googleAnalyticsAdditionalAccess -> Marketer -> Analytics Marketer; googleAnalyticsReadAndAnalyze -> Viewer (no restrictions) -> Analytics Viewer (no restrictions); googleAnalyticsRestrictedAccess -> Viewer (restricted) -> Analytics Viewer (no cost/revenue data). Links made before Jan 4 2023 may differ — check/edit via Admin > linked property > Property Access Management. Changing a Firebase-linked-user's Analytics role/restrictions affects everyone in that Firebase group; persists until the link is deleted. Example: restrict cost/revenue visibility via Admin > Property > Property Access Management > select the Firebase user row > Data restrictions > No Cost Metrics / No Revenue Metrics.

Enhanced audience integration benefits: prepopulates Firebase-exported audiences with up to 30 days of existing data; exports predictive/dynamically-evaluated/time-windowed audiences from Analytics to Firebase. On by default, can be turned off.

Starting from Firebase: upgrading a project that already had Analytics enabled auto-links it to a GA4 property. Enabling Analytics later lets you auto-create a new GA4 property or link to an existing one (requires firebaseanalytics.resources.googleAnalyticsEdit permission, included in Firebase Owner/Editor/Firebase Admin roles). Unlinking in the Firebase console stops data flow to GA4 (disables Analytics tracking for that project).

Create a project: optionally integrate with Analytics at creation — associate with an existing GA account or auto-create "Default Account for Firebase". Firebase users get Analytics roles per the mapping above.

Link/edit/relink/unlink: all done by Firebase Owners under Project settings > Integrations > Google Analytics card (Link / View link / re-link). Takes up to 24h for data to flow after linking, affecting A/B Testing, Crash Reporting, segmentation/targeting features. GA4 only shows Firebase data once a property is linked.

View the history of account/property changes
You need the Editor role to view Change history for an Analytics account or property.

Change history provides a record of changes made to an account over the last 2 years.

View change history

Time: The date and time of the activity
Location type: the Analytics account or property where the change took place
Location name: the name of the Analytics account or property where the change took place
Item type: the type of item that was changed, such as a data stream or Google Ads link
Action: the change, such as create or modified, that was made to the item

Change history also captures some automated system changes.

Entries attributed to [deleted user] indicate that Analytics cannot retrieve an email address because the Google account for the user who made the change has been deleted.

Set the date range

Location: Select the location type or name of the account or property with the changes you want to filter. For properties, this filter is only available if they have subproperties.
Item type: Click the checkbox to select the types of items you want to include.
Action: Choose whether the type of change made was Created, Modified, or Deleted.
Changed by: Enter the email address of whoever made the changes you want to include.

Search the contents

Enter dates using the same format as the column entries.

Explore the Google Analytics guide to learn how to add, edit, and delete users or user groups within your Analytics account.
If you're switching from Universal Analytics to Google Analytics, use the migration tool to copy users to your new Google Analytics property.

You can add users at the Analytics account or property level. The level at which you add a user determines that user's initial access. For example, if you add a user at the account level, then that user also has access to all the properties in the account, with the same set of permissions. If you add a user at the property level, then the user has access to only that property with the permissions you provide. You can change the level of access and permissions for a user at any time. Learn more about Access and data-restriction management.

Users are identified by their email addresses. You can only add users whose email addresses are registered in Google accounts.

To add or modify users or user groups, you need to have the Administrator role at the account or property level. You can add or modify users or user groups at each level for which you have permission.

To delete user accounts or user groups, you need to have the Administrator role at the account level. You can delete users or user groups only at the account level.

Any user with permission can delete any other user. As a safety measure, if you are the last user who has the Administrator role, you cannot delete yourself.

[GA4] Move a property
In this article:
About moving properties
Things to keep in mind
How to move a property
About moving properties

If you need to reorganize your properties in Analytics, you can move them (and their data streams) from one account to another.

Moving properties lets you keep your Analytics implementation current with your business. You might be reorganizing after a merger, after an internal restructuring, or after hiring a new agency.

You move a property from a source account to a destination account.

When you move a property, there are some aspects of the property that are moved with the property such as tag ID, property settings, data streams, reporting data, and property-level integrations. There are also some aspects of the property that remain in the source account such as change history. These are covered in more detail in the next section of this article.

To move a property, you need the Administrator and Editor roles for both the source and destination accounts.
Things to keep in mind
Source account

If the source account no longer contains properties after the move, you can delete the source account. An empty source account still counts against the maximum number of Analytics accounts you can have.

Tagging

The Tracking ID (for example, G-123ABC) does not change, so there’s no need to retag anything.

The source account does not reuse the ID, so the ID remains unique throughout your Analytics environment.

Property permissions

When you move a property, you have two options for how to handle permissions:

Replace existing property permissions with permissions of the destination account. The property will inherit permissions from the destination account.
Keep existing property permissions. The current property permissions are copied along with the property. Users who have account-level access in the source account will have property-level access in the destination account.
Reporting data

All reporting data associated with a property is moved (not copied) to the destination account.

Property settings, and associated configurations and objects

Property settings remain intact when you move a property, as do other settings and associated objects like tracking customizations such as User-ID, Remarketing Audiences and Dynamic Attributes, Custom Definitions, Data Import, and Custom Tables.

Data streams

All data streams associated with a property are moved, and all the data-stream settings remain intact.

[GA4] Troubleshoot tag setup on your website
Identify and fix issues with your tag setup that prevent you from seeing data in Google Analytics

You may not see data from your website in Google Analytics for the following reasons:

Your Google tag is not installed on your website

Your Google tag is not installed on your website

You can install Google Analytics on your website using the Google tag (gtag.js) or Google Tag Manager. Depending on the option you choose, you need to add one or two snippets of code to each page of your website. Learn how to install the Google tag

Note: If you use a content management system or website builder that requires you to use a UA ID (legacy), see Set up Analytics for a CMS-hosted website.
Your Google tag is installed incorrectly

The following are possible reasons why your code might be installed incorrectly:

Google tag (gtag.js)
The Google tag snippet is in the wrong place
The Google tag ID is incorrect
The Google tag contains extra whitespaces or characters
Tag Manager

For more information about troubleshooting your Tag Manager setup, see Troubleshoot issues.

Enable remarketing with Google Analytics data
Learn about the required settings to use Analytics audiences in Ads
 Drive more sales with Google Ads

Use your insights from Google Analytics to get your business in front of the right customers across Search, YouTube, and more with Google Ads.

Get started
Important: Web and app display dynamic remarketing is available in Google Analytics. This feature allows advertisers to transfer dynamic attributes, such as product IDs or price values, directly to Google Ads for dynamic remarketing campaigns. This eliminates the need to manually define and map parameters, simplifying the setup process and enabling more dynamic and relevant ad experiences.
About remarketing

Remarketing lets you re-engage users based on their behavior in your app or on your site. When users fit the behavioral profile for an audience (for example, Reached Level 9), they are added to that audience and are eligible to see ads related to that earlier behavior.

You can create audiences in your Google Analytics properties from any combination of dimensions, metrics, and events (for example, Android users who triggered in_app_purchase events).

Analytics also automatically creates two audiences:

Purchasers: Users who have purchased an app, made an in-app purchase, or made a website purchase
All users: Users who have installed your app or initiated sessions on your website

When you link Analytics to your Google Ads accounts and enable ads personalization:

Any audiences you create in Analytics are automatically exported to those accounts and become available for remarketing on the Google Search Network, Google Display Network, and YouTube.
Analytics backfills those audiences with recently added members and those audiences are available for use in Google Ads within 1 day (on average).
You can view the estimated audience size in Google Ads at any time. Note that for new audiences, while it may take some time for Google Ads to populate audiences to meet the size estimates, you can use those audiences in campaigns in the meantime.

When your data includes user IDs, any audience you create can include users associated with those IDs. The audience will reflect devices on which a user ID was observed, and personalized ads will be displayed only on those devices.

If your data includes user-provided data, any audience exported to your linked Google Ads account will match your consented, hashed customer data with Google data to populate audiences when cookies or other user identifiers are not available. This helps maximize coverage for remarketing efforts, ensuring that your campaigns reach the most relevant audiences.
